content:
There are reports yesterday that Apple has agreed to comply with the EU's "fairer" app tracking transparency rules, after an investigation by the German antitrust regulator.

Apple said it is a voluntary compliance, and as we understand, they will make a total of eight changes to meet the relevant requirements……

Developers often collect far more personal data than the app's functionality requires. Apple refers to this as app tracking: the interests revealed by the apps you install are used to deliver personalized ads to you, whether within apps or on the web. The App Tracking Transparency (ATT) feature gives you the choice of whether this data can be collected and used in this way.

Apple said yesterday that the Federal Cartel Office (FCO) recognizes the value of giving users a choice; in fact, the FCO's report noted that they welcome ATT from a data protection standpoint, and other German privacy regulators hold the same position.

The FCO's objection appears to be that Apple's current prompts make app tracking sound more harmful than it actually is. The iPhone maker will make eight changes to address this—including removing the word "track".

  • Change the color of the graphic element at the top of the prompt from orange to blue
  • Update the ATT prompt to display as a full page
  • Remove the word "track" from the ATT prompt and the personalized ads prompt
  • Change the choice buttons for ATT from "Allow" and "Ask App Not to Track" to "Allow" and "Reject"
  • Allow formatting variations in the ATT prompt (e.g., bold, italic, and bulleted lists)
  • Add an option for developers to display an additional page of information directly within the prompt to provide more GDPR-related information. In fact, developers can already do this by showing their own prompt before the ATT prompt.
  • Allow developers to prompt users again with the ATT prompt one year after the user makes a decision, regardless of whether the choice was "yes" or "no"
  • Make slight adjustments to the wording of the personalized ads prompt for greater clarity, but the effect or meaning of the wording remains unchanged

Apple told us that it is committed to ensuring ATT continues to be available in EU countries, and said the measure has been welcomed by privacy advocacy groups, data protection authorities, and iPhone users.

The company reiterated that its own apps do not display the ATT prompt, because they do not use personal data collected from apps to deliver targeted advertising or measure advertising effectiveness. They emphasized that third-party apps are treated exactly the same way—if third-party apps do not collect such data, they do not need to display the prompt.

9to5Mac's take

This outcome appears to be the best result for everyone. iPhone users will continue to make a choice, but based on a prompt that more accurately reflects the decision they are being asked to make—one between personalized ads and no personalized ads.

This investigation also addressed concerns about Apple's own advertising sales business. The company has made it clear that it does not use data collected by its own apps to deliver personalized ads, nor does it use such data to measure advertising effectiveness.
